output.query: Zinc toxicity hepatic encephalopathy urea cycle inhibition mechanism

results.summary: Excess zinc inhibits arginase, a key urea cycle enzyme, leading to hyperammonemia. Zinc supplementation is widely recommended in liver disease for zinc DEFICIENCY (which is common in cirrhosis), but over-supplementation can paradoxically cause HE by inhibiting ammonia metabolism. Zinc levels should be checked in any cirrhotic patient taking zinc supplements who develops HE without obvious precipitant.
results.title: Zinc excess as a cause of hepatic encephalopathy: case series and mechanism

output.summary: Zinc excess is a recognized but underappreciated precipitant of hyperammonemia. Excess zinc inhibits arginase, a key urea cycle enzyme, leading to impaired ammonia disposal. Case series describe zinc supplementation as a reversible cause of encephalopathy in patients with underlying liver disease. Zinc levels should be checked in patients taking zinc supplements who develop encephalopathy without other obvious precipitant.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe benzodiazepines for anxiety/agitation — they precipitate and prolong HE (use haloperidol or non-pharmacologic measures for agitation).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids — they worsen HE; consider acetaminophen at hepatic-safe dosing for pain.
Do not perform LP before neuroimaging excludes mass effect when the patient has altered mental status.
Do not start oral zinc supplementation for HE without confirming a deficiency (zinc supplementation for HE has weak evidence and is harmful when serum levels are already elevated).

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Amyloid PET has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the issue, not Alzheimer pathology.
DaTscan has no role in HE workup; the question is metabolic encephalopathy, not nigrostriatal degeneration.
FDG PET has no role in HE workup; metabolic encephalopathy is reversible with precipitant control and does not require nuclear functional imaging.

accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade II), primary biliary cholangitis cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, MELD 15) — precipitated by zinc toxicity from OTC supplementation (serum zinc 180 µg/dL inhibits urea cycle arginase) plus constipation.

differential.key_features: Hypothyroidism on levothyroxine; cognitive contribution possible but does not cause asterixis or rapid lactulose response.
UDCA is well tolerated and does not cause encephalopathy.
PBC is an established diagnosis; low serum copper (68) is likely from zinc excess displacing copper rather than Wilson disease.
Acute 2-week course with reversibility on lactulose argues against neurodegeneration.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grading + evidence of liver dysfunction + exclusion of other causes of AMS — ammonia level is supportive only and correlates poorly with grade (AASLD 2014).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.
Zinc has been variously suggested to help (deficient patients) or harm (toxic levels) HE; check a level before supplementing — toxicity precipitates HE by inhibiting urea-cycle arginase.
OTC supplement use is a frequently missed precipitant in cirrhotics; ask about supplements specifically.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Low copper here is the consequence of zinc-induced copper malabsorption (a well-described iatrogenic finding), not Wilson disease. PBC etiology is established.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Pursue Wilson disease workup (24-hour urine copper, ceruloplasmin, slit-lamp KF rings).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: UDCA is not encephalopathic; PBC is stably treated; zinc supplementation is the precipitant.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute encephalopathy to PBC progression or UDCA-related toxicity.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. L. is a 63-year-old woman with primary biliary cholangitis (PBC)-related cirrhosis who presents with a 2-week history of gradually worsening cognitive impairment, personality change, and word-finding difficulty noticed by her husband. He reports she has been more irritable, is repeating conversations, cannot follow a television show she normally enjoys, and has been sleeping 10-12 hours per night with daytime drowsiness. She had one prior grade 1 HE episode one year ago which resolved with lactulose adjustment. Her current lactulose dose had not been adjusted and she has been taking it consistently. She is afebrile with normal vital signs. She denies hematemesis, melena, or abdominal pain. She has no ascites currently. Her PBC is stable on ursodeoxycholic acid with good biochemical response. Review of systems was notable for 3-week history of worsening pruritus and constipation — she has been eating a low-fiber diet to try to reduce pruritus-related discomfort. Laboratory evaluation reveals moderately elevated ammonia at 78 µmol/L, mildly elevated bilirubin, and an unexpectedly elevated serum zinc level of 180 µg/dL (reference 60-120 µg/dL) — she had been self-medicating with OTC zinc supplements for pruritus relief based on online recommendations.
